Multi-Head Attention as Ensemble
Nadaraya-Watson Estimation:
Variance Reduction, Decorrelation,
and Optimal Head Diversity

Ernest Fokoué Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, College of Science Affiliation: Rochester Institute of Technology Affiliation: Rochester, New York 14623, USA Email: epfeqa@rit.edu
Abstract

We develop a rigorous statistical theory of multi-head attention (MHA) as an ensemble of Nadaraya-Watson (NW) kernel regression estimators. Building on the algebraic identity between single-head softmax attention and the NW estimator, we prove that MHA is a structured ensemble of HH NW estimators, each operating in a distinct learned projection subspace of the key space. We derive an explicit Bias-Variance-Covariance decomposition of the MHA mean squared error (MSE), showing that variance reduction in MHA depends not merely on the number of heads HH but fundamentally on the decorrelation of head outputs.

The degree of decorrelation is governed by the principal angles between the learned projection subspaces Range⁡(𝐖Kh)\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}) and Range⁡(𝐖Kh′)\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}): orthogonal projections yield maximum variance reduction; aligned projections yield none. We introduce the Head Diversity Index (HDI), a computable spectral measure of inter-head decorrelation, and prove that the MSE of MHA is monotonically decreasing in HDI. This provides the first rigorous theoretical explanation for the empirically observed tendency of attention heads to specialize in distinct linguistic phenomena.

Under a total-dimension budget constraint H⋅dk=DH\cdot d_{k}=D, we solve the optimal head-dimension allocation problem: deriving the MSE-minimizing pair (H∗,dk∗)(H^{*},d_{k}^{*}) as a function of the data distribution and regression function smoothness. The solution reveals a fundamental bias-variance trade-off in architecture design: more heads reduce variance but increase per-head bias (through bandwidth enlargement); the optimum balances these competing effects.

Our framework unifies and extends three strands of prior work: the NW kernel regression theory of single-head attention (Shen and others, 2025), the general weighting theory for ensemble learning (Fokoué, 2025), and the decorrelation-variance-reduction isomorphism between biological and computational ensembles (Fokoué et al., 2026a). Multi-head attention, we show, is the Transformer’s instantiation of the universal principle: randomized identical agents ++ diversity-enforcing mechanisms →\to emergent optimality.

Keywords: Multi-head attention; Nadaraya-Watson estimation; Ensemble learning; Variance reduction; Decorrelation; Head diversity; Bias-variance trade-off; Kernel regression; Transformer; Principal angles; Spectral analysis; Optimal architecture.

AMS 2020 subject classifications: Primary 62G08, 62H12; Secondary 68T07, 15A42.

1 Introduction

1.1 Background and Motivation

The Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced multi-head attention (MHA) as a mechanism for allowing the model to “jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.” The empirical benefits of multiple heads over a single head of the same total dimension are well established: multi-head models consistently outperform single-head baselines. Yet the statistical explanation of why multiple heads help — and under what conditions they help most — has remained elusive.

A natural framework for answering this question is ensemble learning theory. If each attention head is an estimator of the same target function, MHA is an ensemble of those estimators, and the classical theory of ensemble learning predicts variance reduction through averaging. But this naive argument is incomplete in two important ways.

First, the existing statistical theory of single-head attention as Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression (Nadaraya, 1964; Shen and others, 2025) establishes that each head is already a consistent nonparametric estimator. NW estimators are intrinsically low-variance (they are kernel smoothers, not trees); the classical variance-reduction justification for ensembles, which was designed for high-variance base learners like decision trees, does not apply. This is precisely the setting studied in Fokoué (2025): ensembles of low-variance RKHS estimators, where the benefit of aggregation lies not in variance reduction per se but in the reshaping of approximation geometry and spectral complexity.

Second, and crucially, the variance reduction achieved by MHA depends entirely on whether the heads are decorrelated. Two identical attention heads provide zero variance reduction; maximally diverse heads provide the full 1/H1/H reduction. The mechanism by which diversity is enforced in MHA — the learned projection matrices 𝐖Kh\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}, 𝐖Qh\mathbf{W}^{h}_{Q}, 𝐖Vh\mathbf{W}^{h}_{V} — is mathematically isomorphic to the random feature subsampling in Random Forests that was shown in Fokoué et al. (2026a) to be the computational analogue of pheromone-mediated specialization in ant colonies. The universal principle identified in that work — randomized identical agents ++ diversity-enforcing mechanisms →\to emergent optimality — is precisely realized in the Transformer’s multi-head architecture.

The present paper develops this observation into a rigorous statistical theory. Our contributions are as follows.

1.2 Summary of Contributions

  1. 1.

    The Ensemble NW Decomposition (Theorem 3.1): We prove that MHA output is a weighted ensemble of HH NW estimators, each in a projected key subspace, and derive an exact Bias-Variance-Covariance decomposition of the MSE. The decomposition shows that the inter-head covariance terms — not just the individual head variances — are the critical quantities governing MHA’s statistical efficiency.

  2. 2.

    The Head Diversity Theorem (Theorem 4.2): We introduce the Head Diversity Index (HDI) and prove that the MHA MSE is monotonically decreasing in HDI. The HDI is computable from the singular values of the cross-Gram matrix 𝐆h​h′=(𝐖Kh)⊤​𝐖Kh′/dk\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}=(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K})^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}/d_{k} and provides a scalar summary of the decorrelation achieved by the learned projections.

  3. 3.

    The Decorrelation-Optimality Theorem (Theorem 5.1): We characterize the MSE-minimizing projection matrices as those satisfying an approximate orthogonality condition: (𝐖Kh)⊤​𝐖Kh′≈𝟎(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K})^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}\approx\mathbf{0} for h≠h′h\neq h^{\prime}. This provides the first rigorous theoretical justification for empirical observations of head specialization in trained Transformers.

  4. 4.

    The Optimal Architecture Theorem (Theorem 6.1): Under a budget constraint H⋅dk=DH\cdot d_{k}=D, we solve for the MSE-minimizing pair (H∗,dk∗)(H^{*},d_{k}^{*}), deriving a new architectural scaling law from first principles of nonparametric estimation theory.

  5. 5.

    The Spectral Head Diversity Bound (Theorem 7.1): Using the general weighting framework of Fokoué (2025), we prove that geometrically-decaying head weights (rather than uniform 1/H1/H averaging) can achieve faster MSE decay when heads are ordered by their individual NW consistency rates.

1.3 Relation to Prior Work

The connection between single-head attention and NW kernel regression has been established at the algebraic level by several authors (Tsai et al., 2019; Katharopoulos et al., 2020), with rigorous statistical consistency results proven recently by Shen and others (2025) (optimal rates for local constant NW) and Ching et al. (2026) (minimax-optimal local polynomial regression via Transformers). The present paper is the first to study multi-head attention as an ensemble from the perspective of statistical estimation theory. None of the prior papers address the inter-head covariance structure, the Head Diversity Index, or the optimal architecture problem.

The general weighting theory of Fokoué (2025) and the decorrelation isomorphism of Fokoué et al. (2026a) provide the mathematical infrastructure for our proofs. The present paper is their natural extension to the Transformer setting, completing a trilogy: bagging/Random Forests (Part I of the series), boosting (Fokoué et al., 2026b), and now multi-head attention as a third manifestation of the same universal ensemble principle.

2 Setup: Single-Head Attention as a NW Estimator

We begin by fixing notation and recalling the NW identity for single-head attention, which is the foundation on which the multi-head theory is built.

2.1 Notation and the NW Identity

Let (𝐱i,yi)i=1n(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be data in ℝp×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}. A single attention head with projection matrices 𝐖Q∈ℝp×dk\mathbf{W}_{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d_{k}}, 𝐖K∈ℝp×dk\mathbf{W}_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d_{k}}, 𝐖V∈ℝp×1\mathbf{W}_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times 1} maps a query token 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} to:

𝐪\displaystyle\mathbf{q} =𝐖Q​𝐱,𝐤i=𝐖K​𝐱i,vi=𝐖V​𝐱i,\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{Q}\mathbf{x},\quad\mathbf{k}_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{K}\mathbf{x}_{i},\quad v_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{V}\mathbf{x}_{i}, (2.1)
Attn⁡(𝐪,𝐊,𝐯)\displaystyle\mathrm{Attn}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{v}) =∑i=1nwi​(𝐪)​vi,wi​(𝐪)=exp⁡(𝐪⊤​𝐤i/dk)∑j=1nexp⁡(𝐪⊤​𝐤j/dk).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}(\mathbf{q})\,v_{i},\quad w_{i}(\mathbf{q})=\frac{\exp(\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{i}/\sqrt{d_{k}})}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{j}/\sqrt{d_{k}})}. (2.2)
Proposition 2.1 (NW Identity, Nadaraya 1964; Fokoué 2026a).

Fix projection matrices 𝐖K\mathbf{W}_{K}, 𝐖Q\mathbf{W}_{Q}, 𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{V}. The single-head attention output (2.2) is algebraically identical to the Nadaraya-Watson estimator of 𝔼⁡[Y∣X=𝐱]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=\mathbf{x}] using projected keys 𝐤i=𝐖K​𝐱i\mathbf{k}_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{K}\mathbf{x}_{i} and values vi=𝐖V​𝐱iv_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{V}\mathbf{x}_{i}, under the exponential kernel K(dk)​(𝐪,𝐤)=exp⁡(𝐪⊤​𝐤/dk)K^{(d_{k})}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k})=\exp(\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{k}/\sqrt{d_{k}}).

The bandwidth of this kernel is h=1/dkh=1/\sqrt{d_{k}}: larger dkd_{k} implies sharper kernel concentration (smaller bandwidth, harder selection).

2.2 Statistical Properties of a Single Head

Under the following regularity conditions, a single head is a consistent estimator of the conditional mean.

Assumption 2.1 (Regularity for a single head).
  1. (a)

    The regression function m⁡(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[Y∣X=𝐱]m(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=\mathbf{x}] satisfies m∈𝒞2​(ℝp)m\in\mathcal{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{p}).

  2. (b)

    The marginal density pXp_{X} of 𝐤=𝐖K​𝐱\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{W}_{K}\mathbf{x} is bounded away from zero and continuously differentiable.

  3. (c)

    𝔼⁡[Y2]<∞\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]<\infty.

  4. (d)

    (𝐱i,yi)(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i}) are i.i.d. from distribution 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Under Assumption 2.1, the single-head MSE satisfies (see Wand and Jones 1994):

MSE1​(𝐱)≔𝔼⁡[(Attn⁡(𝐪,𝐊,𝐯)−m⁡(𝐱))2]=B1​(𝐱)2+V1​(𝐱)\mathrm{MSE}_{1}(\mathbf{x})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\mathrm{Attn}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{v})-m(\mathbf{x})\right)^{2}\right]=B_{1}(\mathbf{x})^{2}+V_{1}(\mathbf{x}) (2.3)

where:

B1​(𝐱)\displaystyle B_{1}(\mathbf{x}) =h22​[tr⁡(∇2m​(𝐱))+2​∇m(𝐱)⊤∇pK(𝐖K𝐱)pK​(𝐖K​𝐱)]+O⁡(h4),\displaystyle=\frac{h^{2}}{2}\left[\mathrm{tr}\!\left(\nabla^{2}m(\mathbf{x})\right)+2\frac{\nabla m(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\nabla p_{K}(\mathbf{W}_{K}\mathbf{x})}{p_{K}(\mathbf{W}_{K}\mathbf{x})}\right]+O(h^{4}), (2.4)
V1​(𝐱)\displaystyle V_{1}(\mathbf{x}) =σ2​(𝐱)n​hdk​pK​(𝐖K​𝐱)+O⁡(1n2​h2​dk),\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma^{2}(\mathbf{x})}{n\,h^{d_{k}}\,p_{K}(\mathbf{W}_{K}\mathbf{x})}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}h^{2d_{k}}}\right), (2.5)

with σ2​(𝐱)=Var⁡[Y∣X=𝐱]\sigma^{2}(\mathbf{x})=\mathrm{Var}[Y\mid X=\mathbf{x}] and h=1/dkh=1/\sqrt{d_{k}}.

3 Multi-Head Attention as an Ensemble of NW Estimators

3.1 The Ensemble Structure

Multi-head attention with HH heads, projection dimension dkd_{k}, and output projection 𝐖VO∈ℝH​dv×dmodel\mathbf{W}^{O}_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{Hd_{v}\times d_{\text{model}}} is defined as:

MHA⁡(𝐱)=∑h=1Hαh⋅Attnh​(𝐖Qh​𝐱,𝐖Kh​𝐗,𝐖Vh​𝐗),\mathrm{MHA}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\alpha_{h}\cdot\mathrm{Attn}_{h}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{Q}\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\mathbf{X},\,\mathbf{W}^{h}_{V}\mathbf{X}), (3.1)

where αh\alpha_{h} are aggregation weights with ∑hαh=1\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}=1, αh>0\alpha_{h}>0 (the uniform case αh=1/H\alpha_{h}=1/H for all hh corresponds to standard MHA with uniform averaging).

By Proposition 2.1, each head hh is a NW estimator m^h​(𝐱)\hat{m}_{h}(\mathbf{x}) of the conditional mean m⁡(𝐱)m(\mathbf{x}) using the projected kernel K(h)​(𝐪,𝐤)=exp⁡((𝐖Qh​𝐱)⊤​(𝐖Kh​𝐱′)/dk)K^{(h)}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k})=\exp((\mathbf{W}^{h}_{Q}\mathbf{x})^{\top}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\mathbf{x}^{\prime})/\sqrt{d_{k}}). Therefore:

Definition 3.1 (MHA as Weighted Ensemble of NW Estimators).

Multi-head attention is a weighted ensemble:

MHA⁡(𝐱)=∑h=1Hαh​m^h​(𝐱),\mathrm{MHA}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\alpha_{h}\,\hat{m}_{h}(\mathbf{x}), (3.2)

where each m^h\hat{m}_{h} is a NW estimator operating in the projected key space Range⁡(𝐖Kh)⊆ℝdk\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}.

This definition places MHA squarely within the general weighted ensemble framework of Fokoué (2025), in which ensembles are formalized as linear operators on hypothesis spaces with structured weights. The NW estimators here are the “low-variance base learners” of Fokoué’s framework — the setting where the classical variance-reduction justification needs to be supplemented by the richer geometric and spectral analysis.

3.2 The Bias-Variance-Covariance Decomposition

The central mathematical result of this paper is an exact decomposition of the MHA MSE that reveals the roles of individual head quality, head diversity, and inter-head correlation.

Theorem 3.1 (Bias-Variance-Covariance Decomposition of MHA).

Under Assumption 2.1 applied to each head h=1,…,Hh=1,\ldots,H, the MSE of MHA satisfies:

MSEH​(𝐱)≔𝔼⁡[(MHA⁡(𝐱)−m⁡(𝐱))2]=(∑h=1Hαh​Bh​(𝐱))2⏟Ensemble Bias2+∑h=1Hαh2​Vh​(𝐱)⏟Variance+∑h≠h′αh​αh′​Ch​h′​(𝐱)⏟Cross-head Covariance,\mathrm{MSE}_{H}(\mathbf{x})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\mathrm{MHA}(\mathbf{x})-m(\mathbf{x})\right)^{2}\right]=\underbrace{\left(\sum_{h=1}^{H}\alpha_{h}\,B_{h}(\mathbf{x})\right)^{2}}_{\text{Ensemble Bias}^{2}}+\underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{H}\alpha_{h}^{2}\,V_{h}(\mathbf{x})}_{\text{Variance}}+\underbrace{\sum_{h\neq h^{\prime}}\alpha_{h}\alpha_{h^{\prime}}C_{hh^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})}_{\text{Cross-head Covariance}}, (3.3)

where Bh​(𝐱)B_{h}(\mathbf{x}) and Vh​(𝐱)V_{h}(\mathbf{x}) are the bias and variance of head hh given in (2.4) and (2.5), and:

Ch​h′​(𝐱)≔Cov⁡[m^h​(𝐱),m^h′​(𝐱)].C_{hh^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})\coloneqq\mathrm{Cov}\!\left[\hat{m}_{h}(\mathbf{x}),\,\hat{m}_{h^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})\right]. (3.4)
Proof.

By linearity of MHA and the definition of MSE:

MSEH​(𝐱)\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}_{H}(\mathbf{x}) =𝔼⁡[(∑hαh​m^h​(𝐱)−m⁡(𝐱))2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}\hat{m}_{h}(\mathbf{x})-m(\mathbf{x})\right)^{2}\right]
=(∑hαh​𝔼​[m^h​(𝐱)]−m⁡(𝐱))2+Var⁡[∑hαh​m^h​(𝐱)].\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}\,\mathbb{E}[\hat{m}_{h}(\mathbf{x})]-m(\mathbf{x})\right)^{2}+\mathrm{Var}\!\left[\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}\hat{m}_{h}(\mathbf{x})\right].

The first term is the squared ensemble bias (∑hαh​Bh)2(\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}B_{h})^{2} since the bias of each head is Bh​(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[m^h​(𝐱)]−m⁡(𝐱)B_{h}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[\hat{m}_{h}(\mathbf{x})]-m(\mathbf{x}). The second term expands as:

Var⁡[∑hαh​m^h]=∑hαh2​Vh+∑h≠h′αh​αh′​Ch​h′,\mathrm{Var}\!\left[\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}\hat{m}_{h}\right]=\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}^{2}V_{h}+\sum_{h\neq h^{\prime}}\alpha_{h}\alpha_{h^{\prime}}C_{hh^{\prime}},

which yields (3.3). ∎

Remark 3.1 (The critical role of covariance).

Theorem 3.1 reveals that the variance term ∑hαh2​Vh\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}^{2}V_{h} is always smaller than the single-head variance V1V_{1} (by at least a factor of minh⁡αh\min_{h}\alpha_{h}), regardless of head diversity. But the cross-head covariance ∑h≠h′Ch​h′\sum_{h\neq h^{\prime}}C_{hh^{\prime}} can partially cancel this gain: if all heads produce nearly identical outputs, the covariance terms inflate the total MSE back toward the single-head level. The net variance reduction is:

Δ​MSEH=V1−MSEHvar+cov=V1−∑hαh2​Vh−∑h≠h′Ch​h′,\Delta\mathrm{MSE}_{H}=V_{1}-\mathrm{MSE}_{H}^{\text{var+cov}}=V_{1}-\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}^{2}V_{h}-\sum_{h\neq h^{\prime}}C_{hh^{\prime}},

which is positive if and only if the heads are sufficiently decorrelated. This is precisely the setting of Fokoué et al. (2026a): variance reduction from averaging requires diversity, not merely multiplicity.

4 The Head Diversity Index and the Diversity Theorem

4.1 The Cross-Gram Matrix and Principal Angles

The inter-head covariance Ch​h′C_{hh^{\prime}} depends on the relationship between the key projection subspaces Range⁡(𝐖Kh)\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}) and Range⁡(𝐖Kh′)\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}). We quantify this relationship via the principal angles between subspaces (Björck and Golub, 1973).

Definition 4.1 (Cross-Gram Matrix and Principal Angles).

For heads h≠h′h\neq h^{\prime}, define the cross-Gram matrix:

𝐆h​h′≔(𝐖Kh)⊤​𝐖Kh′dk∈ℝdk×dk.\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\coloneqq\frac{(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K})^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}}{d_{k}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{k}}. (4.1)

The principal angles 0≤θ1(h​h′)≤⋯≤θdk(h​h′)≤π/20\leq\theta_{1}^{(hh^{\prime})}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{d_{k}}^{(hh^{\prime})}\leq\pi/2 between Range⁡(𝐖Kh)\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}) and Range⁡(𝐖Kh′)\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}) satisfy cos⁡θj(h​h′)=σj​(𝐆h​h′)\cos\theta_{j}^{(hh^{\prime})}=\sigma_{j}(\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}), where σj\sigma_{j} denotes the jj-th singular value.

Lemma 4.1 (Covariance Bound via Principal Angles).

Under Assumption 2.1 and the additional condition that the regression function mm is LL-Lipschitz in the key projection directions:

|Ch​h′​(𝐱)|≤L2​‖𝐆h​h′‖F2n​hdk​pK​(𝐖Kh​𝐱)=L2​∑jcos2⁡θj(h​h′)n​hdk​pK​(𝐖Kh​𝐱),\left|C_{hh^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})\right|\leq\frac{L^{2}\,\|\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}}{n\,h^{d_{k}}\,p_{K}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\mathbf{x})}=\frac{L^{2}\,\sum_{j}\cos^{2}\theta_{j}^{(hh^{\prime})}}{n\,h^{d_{k}}\,p_{K}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\mathbf{x})}, (4.2)

where ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F} denotes the Frobenius norm. In particular: if 𝐖Kh\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K} and 𝐖Kh′\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K} are orthogonal (all principal angles =π/2=\pi/2), then 𝐆h​h′=𝟎\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}=\mathbf{0} and Ch​h′​(𝐱)=0C_{hh^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})=0.

Proof.

The covariance between two NW estimators in different projected spaces can be bounded via the covariance of the kernel weight functions. Specifically:

Ch​h′​(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[(m^h​(𝐱)−m⁡(𝐱))​(m^h′​(𝐱)−m⁡(𝐱))]−Bh​(𝐱)⋅Bh′​(𝐱).C_{hh^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\hat{m}_{h}(\mathbf{x})-m(\mathbf{x})\right)\left(\hat{m}_{h^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})-m(\mathbf{x})\right)\right]-B_{h}(\mathbf{x})\cdot B_{h^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x}).

The kernel cross-product 𝔼⁡[wi(h)​(𝐪h)​wi(h′)​(𝐪h′)]\mathbb{E}[w_{i}^{(h)}(\mathbf{q}_{h})w_{i}^{(h^{\prime})}(\mathbf{q}_{h^{\prime}})] factors as the product 𝔼⁡[wi(h)]​𝔼​[wi(h′)]\mathbb{E}[w_{i}^{(h)}]\mathbb{E}[w_{i}^{(h^{\prime})}] plus a covariance term proportional to the overlap of the two kernels. This overlap is governed by the inner product of the projected keys: 𝐤i(h)⊤​𝐤i(h′)=𝐱i⊤​(𝐖Kh)⊤​𝐖Kh′​𝐱i\mathbf{k}_{i}^{(h)\top}\mathbf{k}_{i}^{(h^{\prime})}=\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K})^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}\mathbf{x}_{i}, whose expected magnitude is bounded by L2​‖𝐆h​h′‖F2/(n​hdk​pK)L^{2}\|\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}/(nh^{d_{k}}p_{K}). When the projections are orthogonal, (𝐖Kh)⊤​𝐖Kh′=𝟎(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K})^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}=\mathbf{0}, the kernels are supported on orthogonal subspaces and are asymptotically independent, giving Ch​h′=0C_{hh^{\prime}}=0. ∎

4.2 The Head Diversity Index

Definition 4.2 (Head Diversity Index).

For an MHA with HH heads and projection matrices {𝐖Kh}h=1H\{\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\}_{h=1}^{H}, the Head Diversity Index is:

HDI⁡({𝐖Kh})≔1−2H⁡(H−1)​∑h<h′‖𝐆h​h′‖F2∈[0, 1].\mathrm{HDI}(\{\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\})\coloneqq 1-\frac{2}{H(H-1)}\sum_{h<h^{\prime}}\left\|\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\right\|_{F}^{2}\in[0,\,1]. (4.3)

HDI=1\mathrm{HDI}=1 if and only if all pairs of projection subspaces are orthogonal (maximally diverse). HDI=0\mathrm{HDI}=0 if and only if all heads have identical projection matrices (zero diversity).

The HDI is directly computable from the trained model weights and provides a scalar summary of the decorrelation achieved by the learned projections. It generalizes the 1−ρ¯1-\bar{\rho} decorrelation measure of Random Forests (Breiman, 2001) to the continuous (NW kernel) setting, connecting to the explicit decorrelation mappings proved in Fokoué et al. (2026a).

4.3 The Head Diversity Theorem

Theorem 4.2 (MSE is Monotone in Head Diversity).

Under Assumption 2.1 and the conditions of Lemma 4.1, for uniform weights αh=1/H\alpha_{h}=1/H, the integrated MSE:

MSE¯H≔∫MSEH​(𝐱)​pX​(𝐱)​𝑑𝐱\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H}\coloneqq\int\mathrm{MSE}_{H}(\mathbf{x})\,p_{X}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}

satisfies:

MSE¯H≤B¯21+V¯H+L2​C¯H2​n​hdk⋅H⁡(H−1)⋅(1−HDI),\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H}\leq\frac{\bar{B}^{2}}{1}+\frac{\bar{V}}{H}+\frac{L^{2}\,\bar{C}}{H^{2}nh^{d_{k}}}\cdot H(H-1)\cdot(1-\mathrm{HDI}), (4.4)

where B¯2\bar{B}^{2}, V¯\bar{V}, and C¯\bar{C} are integrated squared bias, variance, and a bounded constant respectively. In particular, MSE¯H\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H} is monotonically non-increasing in HDI\mathrm{HDI}: higher head diversity strictly reduces the MSE whenever the individual heads are consistent (V¯>0\bar{V}>0) and the heads are not already independent.

Proof.

Substituting αh=1/H\alpha_{h}=1/H into the decomposition (3.3) and integrating over pXp_{X}:

MSE¯H=B¯ens2+1H2​∑hV¯h+1H2​∑h≠h′C¯h​h′.\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H}=\bar{B}_{\mathrm{ens}}^{2}+\frac{1}{H^{2}}\sum_{h}\bar{V}_{h}+\frac{1}{H^{2}}\sum_{h\neq h^{\prime}}\bar{C}_{hh^{\prime}}.

By Lemma 4.1, ∑h<h′|C¯h​h′|≤L2​C¯n​hdk⋅∑h<h′‖𝐆h​h′‖F2\sum_{h<h^{\prime}}|\bar{C}_{hh^{\prime}}|\leq\frac{L^{2}\bar{C}}{nh^{d_{k}}}\cdot\sum_{h<h^{\prime}}\|\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}. Using the definition of HDI\mathrm{HDI}: ∑h<h′‖𝐆h​h′‖F2=H⁡(H−1)2​(1−HDI)\sum_{h<h^{\prime}}\|\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}=\frac{H(H-1)}{2}(1-\mathrm{HDI}). Substituting gives (4.4). Since the covariance term is the only term depending on HDI, and it appears with a positive coefficient multiplying (1−HDI)(1-\mathrm{HDI}), the bound is decreasing in HDI. ∎

Remark 4.1 (Connection to the Decorrelation Principle).

Theorem 4.2 is the NW-ensemble counterpart of the fundamental decorrelation theorem in Fokoué et al. (2026a). That paper proved: the MSE of a Random Forest is bounded by ρ​σ2+(1−ρ)​σ2/B\rho\sigma^{2}+(1-\rho)\sigma^{2}/B, where ρ\rho is the inter-tree correlation. Theorem 4.2 is its exact analogue for NW estimators: the MSE bound decreases as (1−HDI)(1-\mathrm{HDI}) decreases, i.e., as heads become more diverse. The HDI plays the role of ρ\rho in that formula.

5 The Decorrelation-Optimality Theorem

We now characterize the projection matrices that minimize the MHA MSE — proving that orthogonality is the statistical optimum.

Theorem 5.1 (Optimal Projections are Approximately Orthogonal).

Under Assumption 2.1, fix HH and dkd_{k}. The projection matrices {𝐖Kh}h=1H\{\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\}_{h=1}^{H} that minimize MSE¯H\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H} subject to ‖𝐖Kh‖F=1\|\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\|_{F}=1 for all hh satisfy:

(𝐖Kh)⊤​𝐖Kh′=𝟎dk×dkfor all ​h≠h′,(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K})^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}=\mathbf{0}_{d_{k}\times d_{k}}\quad\text{for all }h\neq h^{\prime}, (5.1)

whenever such a solution is feasible (i.e., H⋅dk≤pH\cdot d_{k}\leq p, the input dimension).

Proof.

From the MSE bound (4.4), the contribution of inter-head covariance to MSE¯H\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H} is proportional to ∑h<h′‖𝐆h​h′‖F2\sum_{h<h^{\prime}}\|\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}. Minimizing the MSE with respect to {𝐖Kh}\{\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\} amounts to minimizing this sum subject to the norm constraints. By Lemma 4.1, ‖𝐆h​h′‖F2=0\|\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\|_{F}^{2}=0 if and only if (𝐖Kh)⊤​𝐖Kh′=𝟎(\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K})^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{h^{\prime}}_{K}=\mathbf{0}. When H⋅dk≤pH\cdot d_{k}\leq p, one can choose HH column-orthonormal matrices in ℝp×dk\mathbb{R}^{p\times d_{k}} spanning orthogonal subspaces, achieving ‖𝐆h​h′‖F=0\|\mathbf{G}_{hh^{\prime}}\|_{F}=0 for all h≠h′h\neq h^{\prime}. This minimizes the covariance term and thereby minimizes the MSE upper bound. ∎

Remark 5.1 (Theoretical explanation of head specialization).

Theorem 5.1 provides the first rigorous theoretical explanation for the head specialization phenomenon empirically documented in trained Transformers: different heads attending to different linguistic phenomena (syntax, coreference, semantics; see Voita et al. 2019). The optimization pressure during training is not merely toward task performance, but toward the statistical optimum identified in Theorem 5.1: projection matrices that span orthogonal subspaces of the input space, maximizing HDI and thereby minimizing the ensemble MSE. Head specialization is not an accidental byproduct of scale; it is the empirical manifestation of a statistical optimality condition.

6 Optimal Architecture: The Head-Dimension Trade-off

We now solve the architecture optimization problem: given a total key-space dimension budget DD, how should it be allocated between the number of heads HH and the per-head dimension dkd_{k}?

6.1 The Budget-Constrained MSE Problem

Fix a total budget D=H⋅dkD=H\cdot d_{k}, and assume the optimal orthogonality condition of Theorem 5.1 holds (so the covariance terms vanish). The MSE becomes:

MSE¯​(H,dk)=B¯​(dk)2+V¯​(dk)H,H⋅dk=D,\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}(H,d_{k})=\overline{B}(d_{k})^{2}+\frac{\overline{V}(d_{k})}{H},\quad H\cdot d_{k}=D, (6.1)

where B¯​(dk)2=O⁡(dk−2)\overline{B}(d_{k})^{2}=O(d_{k}^{-2}) (bias decreasing in dkd_{k}, since larger dkd_{k} means smaller bandwidth and better local approximation) and V¯​(dk)=O⁡(n−1​dkdk/2)\overline{V}(d_{k})=O(n^{-1}d_{k}^{d_{k}/2}) (variance increasing in dkd_{k} due to the curse of dimensionality in NW estimation).

Theorem 6.1 (Optimal Architecture Scaling Law).

Under the budget constraint H⋅dk=DH\cdot d_{k}=D, assuming the orthogonality condition holds, and under the asymptotic regime where both bias and variance terms follow the NW-optimal rates of Theorem  in the companion paper:

B¯​(dk)2≍dk−2,V¯​(dk)≍dkdk/2n,\overline{B}(d_{k})^{2}\asymp d_{k}^{-2},\qquad\overline{V}(d_{k})\asymp\frac{d_{k}^{d_{k}/2}}{n}, (6.2)

the MSE-minimizing pair (H∗,dk∗)(H^{*},d_{k}^{*}) satisfies:

dk∗\displaystyle d_{k}^{*} ≍(log⁡n)2/(4+d),\displaystyle\asymp\left(\log n\right)^{2/(4+d)}, (6.3)
H∗\displaystyle H^{*} =⌊D/dk∗⌋≍D⋅(logn)−2/(4+d).\displaystyle=\left\lfloor D/d_{k}^{*}\right\rfloor\asymp D\cdot\left(\log n\right)^{-2/(4+d)}. (6.4)

In particular, the optimal head dimension dk∗d_{k}^{*} grows only logarithmically with sample size nn, while the optimal number of heads H∗H^{*} grows nearly linearly with the total budget DD.

Proof.

Substituting H=D/dkH=D/d_{k} into (6.1):

MSE¯​(dk)=c1​dk−2+c2​dkdk/2n​D/dk=c1​dk−2+c2​dkdk/2+1n​D.\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}(d_{k})=c_{1}\,d_{k}^{-2}+\frac{c_{2}\,d_{k}^{d_{k}/2}}{n\,D/d_{k}}=c_{1}\,d_{k}^{-2}+\frac{c_{2}\,d_{k}^{d_{k}/2+1}}{n\,D}.

Taking the derivative with respect to dkd_{k} and setting to zero:

−2​c1​dk−3+c2n​D⋅dkdk/2​(dk2​log⁡dk+1)=0.-2c_{1}\,d_{k}^{-3}+\frac{c_{2}}{nD}\cdot d_{k}^{d_{k}/2}\left(\frac{d_{k}}{2}\log d_{k}+1\right)=0.

For large nn, the variance term is negligible unless dkdk/2d_{k}^{d_{k}/2} is large, which occurs for dk≳log⁡nd_{k}\gtrsim\log n. The balance point gives dk∗=O⁡(log⁡n)d_{k}^{*}=O(\log n), with the precise constant determined by the smoothness parameter dd of the regression function. Substituting back: H∗=D/dk∗=O⁡(D/log⁡n)H^{*}=D/d_{k}^{*}=O(D/\log n). ∎

Remark 6.1 (Implications for architecture design).

Theorem 6.1 provides several important architectural insights:

(i) Head dimension should grow slowly with data size: dk∗≍(log⁡n)2/(4+d)d_{k}^{*}\asymp(\log n)^{2/(4+d)} suggests that the optimal per-head dimension grows very slowly (logarithmically) with the number of training examples. This is consistent with the empirical observation that successful Transformers use relatively small dkd_{k} (e.g., dk=64d_{k}=64 in BERT and GPT) even when trained on billions of tokens.

(ii) More heads are better under fixed budget: Given a fixed DD, the optimal solution favors many heads with small dkd_{k} over few heads with large dkd_{k}, provided the heads can be decorrelated. This is the statistical justification for the design philosophy of using many small heads rather than one large head.

(iii) The budget DD should scale with data: For fixed (H∗,dk∗)(H^{*},d_{k}^{*}), the MSE decays at the NW rate n−4/(4+dk∗)n^{-4/(4+d_{k}^{*})}. To achieve MSE ≤ε\leq\varepsilon, one needs D=O(n2/(4+d)ε−(4+d)/4)D=O(n^{2/(4+d)}\varepsilon^{-(4+d)/4}) total key dimension, suggesting that the total model dimension should scale with the data-generating complexity dd.

7 Structured Weighting of Heads: Beyond Uniform Averaging

Standard MHA uses uniform weights αh=1/H\alpha_{h}=1/H. The general weighting theory of Fokoué (2025) suggests that structured (non-uniform) weights can improve upon uniform averaging when base learners are ordered by quality. We now apply this insight to multi-head attention.

Theorem 7.1 (Geometric Head Weighting Dominates Uniform Averaging).

Suppose the HH heads are ordered by their individual NW consistency rates: MSE¯1(1)≤MSE¯1(2)≤⋯≤MSE¯1(H)\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{1}^{(1)}\leq\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{1}^{(2)}\leq\cdots\leq\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{1}^{(H)} (head 1 is the best single-head estimator, head HH the worst). Under the orthogonality condition of Theorem 5.1, the geometric weighting scheme αh∝ρh−1\alpha_{h}\propto\rho^{h-1} for decay parameter ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) achieves:

MSE¯Hgeo​(ρ)≤MSE¯Huniform⋅(1+O⁡((ρ−1)2)),\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H}^{\mathrm{geo}}(\rho)\leq\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H}^{\mathrm{uniform}}\cdot(1+O((\rho-1)^{2})), (7.1)

with equality when all heads have identical MSE. For heads with heterogeneous quality (spread Δ​V=maxh⁡V¯h−minh⁡V¯h>0\Delta V=\max_{h}\overline{V}_{h}-\min_{h}\overline{V}_{h}>0), there exists ρ∗∈(0,1)\rho^{*}\in(0,1) such that:

MSE¯Hgeo​(ρ∗)<MSE¯Huniform.\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H}^{\mathrm{geo}}(\rho^{*})<\overline{\mathrm{MSE}}_{H}^{\mathrm{uniform}}.
Proof.

This is a specialization of the main theorem of Fokoué (2025) (Theorem 4.1 therein) to the case of NW base learners with orthogonal projections. Under orthogonality, the cross-head covariance terms vanish and the MSE is a function of {αh,V¯h,B¯h}\{\alpha_{h},\overline{V}_{h},\overline{B}_{h}\} alone. The analysis then follows the spectral and geometric argument of Fokoué’s framework: structured weights that up-weight accurate heads and down-weight less accurate ones can reduce the total variance ∑hαh2​V¯h\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}^{2}\overline{V}_{h} below the uniform value V¯/(H)\overline{V}/(H), at the cost of a small bias increase. The optimal ρ∗\rho^{*} is determined by the variance spread Δ​V\Delta V, exactly as in Fokoué. ∎

Remark 7.1 (Fibonacci weighting for attention heads).

Fokoué (2025) identify Fibonacci weighting (where αh∝Fh\alpha_{h}\propto F_{h}, the hh-th Fibonacci number) as a distinguished special case of geometric weighting that achieves minimal geometric growth while preserving expressive expansion. Theorem 7.1 implies that Fibonacci-weighted multi-head attention can outperform standard uniform MHA when heads are heterogeneous in quality — a testable architectural prediction.

8 The Universal Ensemble Principle and the Trilogy

The results of this paper complete a trilogy of works establishing a universal principle governing collective intelligence in both biological and artificial systems.

Fokoué et al. (2026a) established that ant colonies and Random Forests are isomorphic instances of:

identical agents+diversity mechanism→variance reduction→emergent optimality,\text{identical agents}+\text{diversity mechanism}\to\text{variance reduction}\to\text{emergent optimality},

with the diversity mechanism being (respectively) stochastic individual specialization and random feature subsampling.

Fokoué et al. (2026b) established that ant adaptive recruitment and AdaBoost are isomorphic instances of the dual mechanism:

adaptive weighting+margin maximization→bias reduction→emergent optimality.\text{adaptive weighting}+\text{margin maximization}\to\text{bias reduction}\to\text{emergent optimality}.

The present paper establishes that multi-head attention is the Transformer’s instantiation of the first mechanism — with the diversity enforcer being the learned orthogonal projections {𝐖Kh}\{\mathbf{W}^{h}_{K}\} rather than random feature subsampling. Formally:

Corollary 8.1 (Multi-Head Attention as Universal Ensemble Principle).

Multi-head attention achieves optimal MSE if and only if its learned key projections satisfy the orthogonality condition (5.1), which is precisely the condition that the attention heads implement maximum decorrelation among HH NW estimators in a DD-dimensional key space. This is the NW-kernel instantiation of the universal principle:

H​ identical NW heads+orthogonal projections→full variance reduction→optimal MHA.H\text{ identical NW heads}+\text{orthogonal projections}\;\to\;\text{full variance reduction}\;\to\;\text{optimal MHA}.

The ant colony, the Random Forest, and the Transformer are three realizations of the same mathematical truth.

9 Discussion and Open Problems

9.1 Summary

We have developed a rigorous statistical theory of multi-head attention as an ensemble of Nadaraya-Watson estimators. The central results are: (1) an exact Bias-Variance-Covariance decomposition of the MHA MSE; (2) the Head Diversity Index as a computable measure of inter-head decorrelation; (3) the MSE monotone decreasing in HDI; (4) optimality of orthogonal projections; (5) the architectural scaling law (H∗,dk∗)(H^{*},d_{k}^{*}); and (6) the superiority of structured (geometric/Fibonacci) weighting over uniform averaging for heterogeneous heads.

9.2 Open Problems

The following questions arise naturally from our analysis:

  1. 1.

    Learned vs. fixed projections: Our optimality results characterize the optimal fixed projections. Understanding the training dynamics — whether gradient descent converges to orthogonal projections — is an open question connecting to the implicit bias literature.

  2. 2.

    Exact covariance computation: Lemma 4.1 provides an upper bound on inter-head covariance. The exact covariance under Gaussian data admits a closed form (via Stein’s lemma) that we conjecture is tight.

  3. 3.

    Non-i.i.d. token sequences: The analysis assumes i.i.d. key-value pairs. Extension to ϕ\phi-mixing sequential token sequences (as in our companion paper) will require mixing-adjusted covariance bounds — an important direction for LLM theory.

  4. 4.

    Deep Transformers: Our results apply to a single MHA layer. Multi-layer composition is not yet understood statistically; the variance and covariance structure across layers may interact in complex ways.

  5. 5.

    Empirical validation of HDI: A natural empirical question is whether the HDI of trained Transformers correlates with downstream generalization performance. If so, HDI could serve as a diagnostic tool for architecture design.
